entities.name: Alfred Hitchcock
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sir Alfred Joseph Hitchcock (1899–1980) was an English film director and producer who is widely regarded as the 'Master of Suspense' and one of the most influential filmmakers in cinema history. His career spanned six decades, 53 feature films, and both the British and American film industries, producing masterworks that defined the thriller genre.

Hitchcock pioneered visual storytelling techniques—the tracking shot, subjective camera, montage editing, and the 'MacGuffin' plot device—that are now fundamental to cinematic grammar. His British films, including 'The 39 Steps' (1935) and 'The Lady Vanishes' (1938), established his reputation before he moved to Hollywood in 1939.

His American masterpieces form the greatest sustained run of any director: 'Rear Window' (1954), 'Vertigo' (1958), 'North by Northwest' (1959), 'Psycho' (1960), and 'The Birds' (1963). 'Psycho's shower scene—78 camera setups for 45 seconds of screen time—is the most analysed sequence in film history. 'Vertigo' was voted the greatest film ever made in the 2012 Sight & Sound poll.

Despite five Academy Award nominations for Best Director, Hitchcock never won—cinema's most famous oversight. His cameo appearances in his own films, his droll television introductions, and his rotund silhouette made him the most recognisable director in the world. As François Truffaut declared: 'He is the only filmmaker whose name alone can sell a movie.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hitchcock's influence on cinematic grammar and his ability to shape the thriller genre have had a lasting impact on popular culture, with many of his films continuing to be studied and referenced in film schools and popular media.
